# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

I want you to do a review of verify-in-production skill usage. 
You can add other repos (Claudinite certainly) to review their issues.

Are we overly adding "verify in production" tasks that provide no value? Do they work mechanically? Are they created correctly with all the parameters? Are they being closed promptly? Do they close the original task that spawned them? 
I generally ask:

1. Are they working?
2. Are they misused?
3. Are they overused?
4. Are they underused?

If you have other aspects of these questions - investigate those as well.

As an aside - when we have a minor feature implementation - the "test in production" is a great way to validate it. But when we design a larger element of the system - a ~week after everything works *as planned* - the above line of questioning is what we need to do as a follow up.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. that is the rule — this skill is only for the rest: a change whose proof lives somewhere the
repo cannot see yet. You are filing the proof, not doing the work — and the proof itself runs

only where no automatic check can exist.

**The PR must have merged.** This skill runs as a step of the merge, unasked — `merge-to-main`

when the PR opens, not while review is in flight.

under you. Both leave a verification whose premise never reached `main`:

- A **rewritten branch** makes the brief describe a change that no longer exists. #1121 was filed
  against a scope its PR then dropped; the verification was moot before the merge it waited on.
- A **rejected PR** is worse, because the queue cannot tell it from a merge. A blocked item
  releases on its blocker being *closed*, and nothing reads `merged` — so the item goes ready,
  reads an `In-production-when:` that can never become true, pushes `Not-before:` forward by
  `Retry-every:` without comment, and repeats indefinitely. No janitor rule reclaims it: the
  stale-ready sweep cannot see an item sleeping on a future `Not-before`, and the
  stuck-dependency sweep exempts an item whose blockers have closed.

So there is no such thing as filing this early and letting the queue sort it out. Wait for the
merge, then read **what actually landed** — the merged diff, not the branch you remember writing.

## First: does this file anything at all?

Most changes **file nothing.** Run the test in this order and stop at the first answer:

1. **Did you watch it work in this session?** Then it is proven. File nothing.
2. **Did a test that ran prove it?** A unit test, a CI job, an executable-requirements or UI

   that comes back.
3. **Does the change have an observable effect at all?** A comment, a design doc, a README, a
   rename with no behavioural edge, a refactor a passing suite already pins. File nothing.
4. **Otherwise: where does its effect first become observable?** If the answer is a place and a
   moment — a member repo once it converges, a site once it deploys, a session once it reloads
   its rules — that is what you file.

The bar is *could not be watched now*, not *would be nice to double-check*. A verification
filed for a change already covered by a test is a wasted run re-proving what the suite proved.

## What you file

**A deferred request** — the same ad-hoc lane `/do-later` rides, so the queue does the waiting,
the running and the lifecycle; nothing here adds machinery beside it. One issue, titled

block on the first lines of the description**, ahead of your prose — the same placement
[`/do-later`](../do-later/SKILL.md) files under, and what gives the retry below one place to
rewrite `Not-before:`. Then say what changed and why it could not be watched now.

  run can make**: an API response, a file at a URL, an issue's state. "Issue #100 on that repo

  automatic check can exist may `Verify:` name a person's step, spelled out exactly.

You are auditing "Verify in production" (VIP) issues in the GitHub repo missingbulb/Claudinite — issues filed by the verify-in-production skill, which files a deferred verification after a PR merges. Your GitHub access covers missingbulb/Claudinite and missingbulb/Shepherd only; use the GitHub MCP tools (load schemas first via ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__github__issue_read"). Do NOT use search tools; read each issue directly with issue_read (method get, then get_comments, and get_parent to check sub-issue linkage).

The skill's contract for each VIP issue (what "created correctly" means):
- Title `Verify in production: <change>`.
- Body starts with a field block on the FIRST lines: `Original-issue: #N`, `In-production-when: <artifact to read, never a duration>`, `Verify: <assertion with pass condition, machine-readable>`, `Not-before: <ISO instant>`, `Retry-every: <duration>`, `Model: sonnet`. No `Blocked-by:` (filed after merge).
- Label `task:origin:ad-hoc` applied.
- The VIP issue must be a SUB-ISSUE of the Original-issue (check via get_parent).
- Filed only AFTER the PR merged.
- Convergence playbook: if live → verify; pass = comment evidence + close completed; fail = reopen Original-issue with comment + close VIP completed. Not yet live → rewrite Not-before to now+Retry-every, clear task:status:* label, leave open, no comment.

Audit these issues in missingbulb/Claudinite: 1091, 1095, 1112, 1113, 1121, 1124, 1128, 1137, 1154, 1160, 1161, 1171, 1184, 1220, 1229. Note: 1091 and 1128 are meta-issues ABOUT the skill itself (its design, and a filing-before-merge bug) — summarize what they decided in 2-3 sentences each rather than field-auditing them.

For each real VIP issue record:
1. Field block: present? all 6 fields? any malformed (In-production-when that is a duration/merge, Verify without a pass condition, missing Model, etc.)?
2. Labels: task:origin:ad-hoc present? Any anomaly (e.g. legacy labels claude-queued/task:done/task:blocked, labeled done but still open)?
3. Sub-issue parent = Original-issue? (get_parent)
4. Lifecycle: created when, current state, closed when (latency in days), how many retry/run cycles visible in comments, currently parked needs-human? If open since >5 days, why (from comments)?
5. Outcome/value: did the verification PASS (merely re-confirmed the change worked — no fault found), FAIL and reopen the original (found a real fault — name it), get closed not_planned/rejected, or is it still pending? Was the original issue actually reopened on failure?
6. Any mechanical misbehavior: Not-before re-armed from the old value instead of now, comment spam on retries, scheduler never adopting it, wrong close reason, etc.

Write your full per-issue findings to /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Shepherd/05913db3-8428-5927-bc61-c9896f37cd3d/scratchpad/vip-audit-batch-A.md and end with a summary table plus aggregate counts: N created correctly / N with field defects / N sub-issue-linked / N passed-confirm-only / N found-real-fault / N not_planned / N still open / median close latency. Your final reply should contain the aggregate summary (the file holds the detail).

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. {"number":1091,"title":"A change that can only be proven in production files its own verification, automatically","body":"Today the loop that proves a change actually works stops at the merge. Anything whose effect only appears somewhere else — a vendored pack reaching a member, a deployed site, a prose rule that only exists in the *next* session — is verified when the owner happens to ask for it, or not at all. Yesterday's checkbox rule is the example: it landed green, and it took the owner asking to find out whether it closed a real issue on a real repo.

`basics/RULES.md` already says the right thing twice — *watch it work now*, and *when verifying now is genuinely impossible, make the follow-up a mechanism that comes to you*. What is missing is the mechanism, and the discipline of reaching for it without being asked.

**Land two things in `basics`:**

- A **skill** that fires at the end of a change, beside the conversation capture, and decides whether the change is one whose proof lives in production. When it is, it files a verification issue naming the production condition and the assertion. The discernment is the substance: a change already proven by a test that ran, a comment, a design doc, a UI feature with an executable-requirements test, anything watched working this session — none of those file anything.
- A **task** that picks those issues up, re-derives whether the change is live yet, and either runs the assertion or leaves the issue for the next run. Not live yet is silence, not a comment; a condition that never comes true gives up at a stated date rather than waiting forever.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

{"number":1112,"title":"Verify in production: a member's un-converged workflow still starts a scheduler run through the `tick.mjs` shim","body":"#877 renamed `engine/scheduler/queue/tick.mjs` to `scheduler-run.mjs` and left a shim at the old path (DESIGN decision 27, landed in #1108 / `a9a783e`).

**Why this could not be watched now.** The two halves of the change reach a member on different clocks. The mount refreshes on a converge; `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml` is the one path a converge cannot push, so it lands later as a pull request somebody merges. The window this shim exists for — **new mount, old workflow, still naming `tick.mjs`** — therefore only opens once a member has converged, and is only exercised at that member's next hourly scheduler run. At the time of writing GoogleCalendarEventCreator had the old mount and the old workflow, so the window had not opened yet.

A synthetic version of it is already covered: the `old-workflows` rehearsal fixture converges a member holding the previous workflow shape, and `engine-tests/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run-entry-shim.test.mjs` pins that the shim starts the run and that `scheduler-workflow-shape` accepts either spelling. What no test can show is a real member's scheduler workflow running green through it.

If this fails, every member in that window has a queue that has silently stopped — nothing instantiates standing items, nothing readies blocked ones, nothing reclaims a dead claim — with no run left to report it.

Original-issue: #877
In-production-when: any member repo whose `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run.mjs` exists AND whose `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml` still runs `queue/tick.mjs`. Read both files on that repo's default branch. If no member is in that state — every member either still has the old mount, or has already merged the new workflow — the window has not opened and this is not yet live.
Verify: that member's most recent completed `claudinite-scheduler.yml` run, started after the mount converged, concluded `success`, and its log carries the shim's own line `invoked as \`tick.mjs\`, which is the old name for the scheduler run`. A pass is that line plus a green conclusion. A failure is any conclusion other than `success`, or a run whose log shows the entry point could not be found.
Not-before: 2026-08-20T15:00:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day

---

**Instructions for the run.** You decide nothing here; execute this playbook.

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real files on real member repos. Never infer it from a merge, a green canon run, or elapsed time.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the evidence you actually read — the member, the run URL, the log line — and close this issue as completed. Fails: reopen #877 with a comment saying what was asserted, what happened instead and where you read it; comment here linking that; close this issue as completed.
3. **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by one day, re-apply `claude-task` and `claude-model:sonnet`, and leave this issue open. No comment; the bumped field is the record.

One extra exit worth taking: if every member has merged its workflow pull request and none was ever observed mid-window, the window closed without incident. Say so, note that the shim's retirement condition (no member's workflow still names `tick.mjs`) is now met, and close this as completed.

{"number":1113,"title":"Verify in production: members re-stamp with date-anchored versions","body":"#1105 changed `ENGINE_VERSION` and every pack's `version` from a plain integer to a date-anchored string (`'60820.1'`), and widened every reader to take both. What that changes for a member is the shape of a value in **its own** `.claudinite-checks.json` — the stamp the update flows write and the fleet surfaces read.

It could not be watched in the session that landed it, for one reason: a member's stamp only moves when that member converges, which happens on its own nightly cycle. The canary rehearsal ([run 32371130795](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32371130795)) did prove the path end to end — a legacy-stamped member through both flows, mount self-test green — but on **one** repo, against the branch. What is unproven is the fleet: that every member's next converge re-stamps rather than parking, and that a member sitting mid-migration (new engine, packs not yet updated) is not left in a state its own vendored readers reject.

Original-issue: #1100
In-production-when: `missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary`'s `.claudinite-checks.json` on its default branch has `claudinite.engineVersion` matching `^\d{5,6}\.\d+$` rather than a bare integer.
Verify: read the same file on every member the fleet-roster tracker lists. Pass = every member's `claudinite.engineVersion` and every value in `claudinite.packVersions` is a date-anchored string, and no member has an open `needs-human` update PR whose reason mentions a version. Fail = any member still stamping a bare integer more than two of its own converge cycles after this landed, or any member parked with a version-shaped failure — name the member and quote the stamp.
Blocked-by: #1105
Not-before: 2026-08-22T06:00:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day

**For the run.**

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real file over the API. Never infer it from this issue having merged, from a green Actions run, or from elapsed time.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the stamps you actually read, member by member, and close this issue as completed. Fails: reopen #1100 with a comment saying what was asserted, what you found and where you read it; comment here linking that; close this issue as completed.
3. **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by one day, re-apply `claude-task` and `claude-model:sonnet`, leave this issue open. No comment — the bumped field is the record.

Note for a failing case: the tolerance in `engine/version.mjs` means a member holding a legacy integer is *behind*, never *broken*. A member still stamping integers is a converge that is not running, not a format that is not parsing — diagnose it as the former first.

input.prompt:
You are auditing "Verify in production" (VIP) issues — issues filed by the verify-in-production skill, which files a deferred verification after a PR merges. Your GitHub access covers missingbulb/Claudinite and missingbulb/Shepherd only; use the GitHub MCP tools (load schemas first via ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__github__issue_read"). Do NOT use search tools; read each issue directly with issue_read (method get, then get_comments, and get_parent to check sub-issue linkage).

The skill's contract for each VIP issue (what "created correctly" means):
- Title `Verify in production: <change>`.
- Body starts with a field block on the FIRST lines: `Original-issue: #N`, `In-production-when: <artifact to read, never a duration>`, `Verify: <assertion with pass condition, machine-readable>`, `Not-before: <ISO instant>`, `Retry-every: <duration>`, `Model: sonnet`. No `Blocked-by:` (filed after merge).
- Label `task:origin:ad-hoc` applied.
- The VIP issue must be a SUB-ISSUE of the Original-issue (check via get_parent).
- Filed only AFTER the PR merged.
- Convergence playbook: if live → verify; pass = comment evidence + close completed; fail = reopen Original-issue with comment + close VIP completed. Not yet live → rewrite Not-before to now+Retry-every, clear task:status:* label, leave open, no comment.

Audit these issues: in missingbulb/Claudinite: 1388, 1391, 1396, 1401, 1455, 1458, 1460, 1467, 1469, 1476. In missingbulb/Shepherd: 324. Note: 1388 appeared with NO labels at all in a search result — dig into whether it was ever adopted by the scheduler or is stranded.

For each issue record:
1. Field block: present? all 6 fields? any malformed (In-production-when that is a duration/merge, Verify without a pass condition, missing Model, etc.)?
2. Labels: task:origin:ad-hoc present? Any anomaly?
3. Sub-issue parent = Original-issue? (get_parent)
4. Lifecycle: created when, current state, closed when (latency in days), how many retry/run cycles visible in comments, currently parked needs-human? If open since >5 days, why (from comments)?
5. Outcome/value: did the verification PASS (merely re-confirmed the change worked — no fault found), FAIL and reopen the original (found a real fault — name it), get closed not_planned/rejected, or is it still pending? Was the original issue actually reopened on failure?
6. Any mechanical misbehavior: Not-before re-armed from the old value instead of now, comment spam on retries, scheduler never adopting it, wrong close reason, etc.

Write your full per-issue findings to /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Shepherd/05913db3-8428-5927-bc61-c9896f37cd3d/scratchpad/vip-audit-batch-C.md and end with a summary table plus aggregate counts: N created correctly / N with field defects / N sub-issue-linked / N passed-confirm-only / N found-real-fault / N not_planned / N still open / median close latency. Your final reply should contain the aggregate summary (the file holds the detail).

{"number":1253,"title":"Verify in production: the dashboard's lead block and its day picker","body":"#1251 landed a lead region on both dashboard pages: a **Start here** card naming the one piece of work most worth doing, priced by what its park asks of a person, and — on the fleet page — the morning brief with a `‹ ›` picker back through earlier days.

The ranking, the pricing and the card's own rendering are covered by unit tests that ran. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. {"number":1128,"title":"verify-in-production files before the PR merges, and a rejected PR strands the verification forever","body":"The owner's call, from #1121: **a verification follow-up is never created before the PR has merged.** Sometimes PRs are rejected.

#1121 is the example. It was filed at 15:04 against the branch's then-current scope (a full retirement of the classification *and* the conversation surface, which really would have opened an old-pack/new-engine skew window). The branch was then rewritten to pack-only and #1118 merged at 15:20 with the conversation surface untouched. The verification's premise never existed in `main`. A human closed it by hand twelve minutes later.

## Why the current skill invites this

`packs/basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md` says it *"fires automatically at the end of a change"*, and `packs/basics/RULES.md:68` says to file it *"as part of finishing the change"*. A session that has written the code and opened the PR reads "the end of a change" as **now**.

The template then makes filing early the documented path: `Blocked-by: #` (line 44) only makes sense if the PR is still open when you write it. That field exists to accommodate the premature file.

`packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md` already has it right — step 7, after the merge at step 4. The two entry points disagree.

## Why a rejected PR is worse than a wrong premise

`Blocked-by` waits on the blocker being **closed**. Nothing reads `merged`.

`engine/scheduler/queue/readiness.mjs:22`
```js
const blockersDone = blockedBy.every((n) => stateOf(n) === 'closed');
```

A rejected PR is `closed`, so it releases the item exactly as a merge does. What follows:

1. The item goes ready and runs.
2. It reads `In-production-when:` against an artifact that can never become true — the change never landed.
3. "Not yet live" → push `Not-before:` forward by `Retry-every:`, re-apply the labels, leave it open, and per the skill's line 87 post **no comment**: *"No comment; the bumped field is the record."*
4. Forever.

Nothing reclaims it:

- **Janitor rule A** (stale-ready, `janitor-rules.mjs:29`) cannot see it — it is sleeping on a future `Not-before`, never `task:ready`.
- **Janitor rule C** (stuck-dependency, `janitor-rules.mjs:67`) **explicitly exempts** it at line 72, `if (blockedBy.every((n) => stateOf(n) === 'closed')) return false;` — its own comment says *"Sleeping items (a future `Not-before`, blockers closed) never match: waiting for a time is the mechanism working."*

So a verification filed against a PR that gets rejected is a silent `sonnet` run every `Retry-every`, indefinitely, proving a change that does not exist. It is silent by design, which is what makes it hard to notice.

## The change

Move the trigger and remove the field that accommodated the early file:

- [ ] The skill fires **after the merge**, not at the end of the change — description, intro, and the `RULES.md:68` sentence.
- [ ] Drop `Blocked-by:` from the template and its bullet. Filed post-merge there is nothing to block on; `Not-before:` still does the real waiting. Nothing is ever in production before a merge, so there is no case where filing early is correct — a single structural answer means delete the field.
- [ ] State the rejected-PR case explicitly: a PR that closed unmerged files nothing.
- [ ] `merge-to-main` step 7 becomes the named trigger rather than one of two readings.
- [ ] Bump `packs/basics` and `packs/git-github`.

Out of scope, worth its own decision: whether the queue should refuse a work item whose `Blocked-by` names a PR that closed unmerged. That treats the symptom; if nothing is filed pre-merge the case cannot arise.

2026-08-21T05  {"scheduler":1,"executor":1,"agentic":0,"failed":0}

```
2026-08-21  commits=1  linesAdded=103443  linesRemoved=0
```

```
usage-fold [#1172]: this checkout's history starts at 2026-08-21 — days before it carry no commit or line counts
```

2026-07-23  [null, null, null]
2026-07-24  [null, null, null]
```

Each day is an object whose tuple is under `totals`; indexing the object gave `undefined` for every field, which is indistinguishable from "no key" unless you look. {"number":1455,"title":"Verify in production: a member's executor still starts on the single ready trigger","body":"`1295776` (#1450) removed the legacy `task:ready` trigger from the executor workflow, leaving `task:status:waiting-for-executor` and `task:urgent`.

**Why this could not be watched at merge time.** The suite proves the stub's content and the rehearsal proves a consumer converges green against it, but neither executes a GitHub Actions workflow. The changed behaviour — *does a member's executor still wake on a readied item?* — only runs in a member repo, and only after its converge opens a workflow PR that a person merges, because `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot push. Its failure mode is silent in the direction that matters: a trigger that no longer matches means the label event starts nothing, and the queue drains only on the hourly scheduler dispatch, which looks like ordinary latency rather than a break.

Model: sonnet

Original-issue: #1449
In-production-when: `missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary`'s `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml` on its default branch does NOT contain the string `task:ready`.
Verify: on that member, find a `[claudinite-work]` item that reached a terminal status (`task:status:done`, `task:status:rejected`, or any `task:status:needs-human-*`) after that file landed, and read the executor run that claimed it — its `event` must be `issues`, not `workflow_dispatch`. A pass is at least one such item whose claim comment names an `actions-` executor whose run was started by the label event. An item drained only by a `workflow_dispatch` run is NOT a pass: that is the scheduler's drain covering for a trigger that never fired, which is exactly the silent failure this checks for. Zero items in the window is "not yet live", never a pass.
Not-before: 2026-08-31T08:00:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day

## The playbook — the run decides nothing beyond what is written here

1. Read `In-production-when:` against Canary's real workflow file on its default branch. A merge here is not the condition, and neither is elapsed time — that file moves only when somebody merges that member's own PR.
2. **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by `Retry-every:`, clear this issue's `task:status:*` label, leave it open. No comment; the bumped field is the record.
3. **Live** → run `Verify:`.
   - **Passes** → comment the evidence actually read (the item number, its terminal label, the executor run URL and its `event`) and close this issue as completed.
   - **Fails** → reopen #1449 with what was asserted, what happened instead and where you read it; comment here linking that; close this issue as completed. Finding the fault is this run doing its job.
   - **Cannot read the member** → park `task:status:needs-human-action` naming exactly which read you could not make. A Claude Code Remote session can widen its own GitHub scope with `add_repo`; try that before parking.

## What landed and why this could not be watched here

#1468 added janitor rule G, the ended park. `packs/claudinite-tasks/tasks/task-janitor/queue-sweep.mjs` reads each `Ends-when:` target through the **issues** endpoint and derives the item's terminal status from merged-ness:

```js
resolutions.set(endsWhen, target?.state !== 'closed' ? null
  : (target.pull_request?.merged_at ? 'merged' : 'closed'));
```

`merged` → the item closes `task:status:done` / `completed`. Not merged → `task:status:rejected` / `not_planned`.

Every test covering this drives a fake GitHub, so the tests prove the *logic* and assume the *payload*. If `pull_request.merged_at` is absent from that endpoint's response, the expression silently takes the else branch for every ended park: **work that landed gets reported as a run that never happened**, with nothing red anywhere. That is precisely the failure the merged/closed distinction exists to prevent, so the assumption is worth one real read.

The session that wrote it could not make that read — this sandbox's proxy denies `api.github.com` (403). An Actions run can.

1. `In-production-when:` is already true — the artifacts exist. Go straight to `Verify:`. Do not infer the answer from the merge, from a green run, or from documentation; make the two reads.

### #1091 — skill design (closed completed, 2026-08-20, via PR #1092)
Established the VIP mechanism: a skill fires at the end of a change and decides whether its proof lives only in
production (anything already watched working — a test that ran, a doc, a UI change with an executable-requirements
test — files nothing); when it does, it files a verification issue naming the production condition and the
assertion. A companion task picks those issues up, re-derives whether the change is live, and either runs the
assertion or leaves the issue for the next pass — "in production" is defined per-issue in the body, never in
config. Closed same day; #1095 was filed as the mechanism's own production verification.

### #1128 — filing-before-merge bug (closed completed, 2026-08-20, via PR #1131)
Diagnosed from #1121: the skill said "fires at the end of a change", so sessions filed VIPs before the PR merged,
and the template's `Blocked-by:` accommodated that; since the queue releases a blocker on *closed* (not *merged*),
a rejected PR would release the item into a silent, indefinite sonnet retry loop verifying a change that never
landed, which no janitor rule reclaims. Decision: the skill fires only **after** the merge (merge-to-main step 7
is the named trigger), `Blocked-by:` is deleted from the template, and a PR closed unmerged files nothing. Fixed

content.text:
# Verify-in-production review — 36 verifications audited (35 in Claudinite, 1 in Shepherd), every issue read individually

**Verdict up front: the front half of the mechanism works and is improving; the back half — the queue actually running the verification and closing the loop — is where it breaks.** Since the skill was born on Aug 20, its scheduled runs have caught exactly **one real production fault**, while **at least ten verifications were stranded, mis-closed, or silently forgotten** by the machinery that was supposed to run them. The skill's biggest proven value so far is ironic but real: it kept finding faults *in itself*, driving 4 corrective iterations in 10 days.

Base rate: ~153 commits landed on Claudinite's `main` in the window vs 36 verifications filed — roughly 1 in 4 merges. Full per-issue detail is in the three audit files (`vip-audit-batch-A/B/C.md` in the scratchpad).

## 1. Are they working?

**Filing: yes.** 34/36 are correctly sub-issue-linked to their original issue (misses: [#1124](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1124), [#1351](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1351)). Field-block compliance climbed steadily: the Aug 20–22 cohort had 7/13 with defects (missing `Model:`, legacy `Blocked-by:`), while the post-Aug 30 cohort ([#1458](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1458), [#1467](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1467), [#1469](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1469)) is fully to contract. Each contract tightening traced to a fault the previous cohort exposed — that's the discipline working as designed.

**Executing and closing: no.** The failure modes, each hit at least once:

- **Never adopted**: [#1388](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1388) wrote its `task:origin:ad-hoc` mark as body *prose* instead of applying the label — zero labels, zero runs, 3+ days past its `Not-before`, invisible forever.
- **Stranded by the label migration**: [#1112](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1112) and [#1113](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1113) still wear legacy `claude-queued`; zero retries in ~11 days.
- **Never re-adopted after their hold expired**: [#1267](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1267) is 6 days past its `Not-before` with zero pickups; [#1349](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1349)/[#1351](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1351) 5 days. The delayed-entry lane appears to never come back for sleeping items — this looks like a live queue bug, distinct from the label strands.
- **Adopted then dead**: [#1396](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1396) was queued the same minute as its sibling [#1391](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1391) (which ran and closed); 1396 has had zero activity across 3 retry windows.
- **Passed but never closed**: [#1220](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1220) and [#1265](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1265) verified successfully, but MCP-only sessions couldn't run `converge-item.mjs` and hand-set a `task:done` *label* without closing — which also hides them from the leash bot, so nothing will ever return.
- **The retry-from-stale-value bug**: [#1160](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1160) re-fired hourly instead of daily for ~5 days. Fixed Aug 30 ([#1457](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1457)); #1458 is the pending production check of that fix.

## 2. Are they misused?

Not by intent — by *other machinery not respecting the contract*:

- **Janitor sweeps closed two verifications citing the wrong issue**: [#1161](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1161) and [#1253](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1253) were closed by a stale-park sweep whose comment cites #1154 — a *different* verification. Their assertions were never checked; the owed verification was silently discarded.
- [#1401](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1401) closed `completed` without ever running — `not_planned` in `completed` clothing.
- Convergence runs **rewrote issue bodies and destroyed the field block** ([#1343](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1343), [#1460](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1460)) — survivable only because they closed immediately.
- Agents hitting the same converge-script gap resolved it **three different ways** (close per playbook / fake a done label / walk away) — the VIP playbook and the queue's converge rules contradict each other and each session improvises.

## 3. Are they overused?

**Moderately — two specific filing classes provide no value:**

- **Watchable now**: #1460 was filed and then *hand-verified 12 minutes later* — the "could not be watched now" bar wasn't really met; that check belonged in the merging session.
- **Structurally unobservable from the runner**: the dashboard/`github.io` verifications ([#1184](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1184), [#1288](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1288), [#1253](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1253)) sit behind an egress block, and cross-repo ones ([#1268](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1268), [#1291](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1291)) behind MCP scope. In one Aug 24 executor batch, **5 of 7 claimed items parked on environment limits**, burning sessions to discover the same walls. These degrade into `needs-human` parks — a human's memory with extra steps, exactly what the skill exists to avoid. The skill should refuse to file (or file the explicit human-step form) when the runner can't read the artifact.

The 11 confirm-only passes are *not* overuse evidence — a verification that passes did its job. The 1-fault-in-36 catch rate reads low, but #1220's catch was a real one (Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN` 403s on repository variables, so the operator hold is inert in production; reopened [#1214](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1214), still open), and #1460 surfaced a residual gap that became [#1461](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1461).

## 4. Are they underused?

Per-change in Claudinite: no. Two structural gaps though:

- **The only trigger is `merge-to-main`.** Shepherd has 1 verification against 96 commits — most of those are automated deliveries that never pass through the skill. Probably fine (tasks watch their own runs), but any interactive merge done outside the LGTM flow silently skips the decision.
- **Your aside names the real hole.** The skill files *point assertions* — "artifact X reads Y." There is no mechanism for the ~week-later *design retrospective* on a larger element: "now that it all works as planned, is it working, misused, overused, underused?" This very review happened only because you remembered to ask. That's precisely the class of follow-up the basics pack says must "come back on its own, never a human's memory" — and it has no lane.

---

Immediate repairs the audit surfaced: hand-label #1388; re-adopt #1112/#1113; close the verified-but-open #1220/#1265; re-file or re-arm the wrongly-closed #1161/#1253; investigate the delayed-entry re-adoption gap and #1396's stall. Durable fixes: a janitor guard (never close a VIP without evidence naming *its* `Verify:`), a converge path MCP-only sessions can actually complete, a filing bar amendment (runner-readable artifacts only), and a `design-retrospective` follow-up class for larger elements.

input.body:

content.content:
1	---
2	name: do-later
3	description: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
4	---
5	
6	# /do-later — defer a change into a chained request run
7	
8	The owner has spotted a change that should happen **after** the work in front of
9	them. Doing it now derails the session; an ordinary issue waits for somebody to
10	remember it. This files it as an **ad-hoc request** (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §16):
11	an issue the queue picks up on its own, held behind what is still in flight.
12	
13	You are filing work, not doing it. Touch no source file, open no branch.
14	
15	## What you write
16	
17	**One issue, well defined.** The run that implements it will never see this
18	conversation — the issue body is the whole brief. State the change, the files or
19	surfaces it touches if you know them, what "done" looks like, and anything the
20	owner ruled out. Size it to its idea; a rename is a sentence.
21	
22	**Every field a run reads is one block on the first lines of the description**,
23	above the marker and ahead of your prose — the waits and the parameters together,
24	verbatim in this spelling:
25	
26	```
27	Blocked-by: #<what this waits on>
28	Not-before: <ISO instant this may first run>
29	Model: <opus | sonnet | haiku>
30	Automerge: <policy>
31	Task: <pack>/<task>
32	
33	<!-- filed by /do-later -->
34	
35	<the brief>
36	```
37	
38	Write only the lines the deferral actually has; each is explained below. A field
39	further down the body still parses, but nobody editing the issue can then see what
40	the run will do, and a retry that rewrites `Not-before:` has no one place to write
41	it — #1160 carried its model six paragraphs below its waits.
42	
43	The two waits compose: an issue carrying both sleeps until every blocker has
44	closed **and** the moment has passed.
45	
46	**What issue it waits on**, first match wins:
47	
48	1. the issue of the **previous `/do-later` you filed in this session** — that is
49	   the chain the owner asked for, each deferral behind the last;
50	2. otherwise the **pull request** the session's work is on, if one is open;
51	3. otherwise the **issue** the session is working on;
52	4. otherwise nothing — omit the field, and say in your reply that it queues
53	   immediately.
54	
55	Only ever name blockers that will actually *close* — a merged PR does, a branch
56	does not. If you filed an earlier `/do-later` this session but no longer have its
57	number, find it by its marker line among the repo's open issues rather than
58	falling back to (2).
59	
60	**What moment it waits on.** A deferral the owner words as a *time* — "check
61	tomorrow", "in a week", "not until after the release" — waits on an instant, and
62	`Blocked-by:` cannot express it. That is `Not-before:`, and it is the queue's own
63	wait field rather than a parameter: it is honoured whether or not the author holds
64	push access. Give it an ISO-8601 instant resolved against today's date
65	(`Not-before: 2026-08-28T09:00:00Z`) — the next scheduler run adopts the issue,
66	holds it blocked, and releases it on the first hourly pass after that instant.
67	A time-worded deferral is never case 4: it waits on the moment even when no issue
68	or PR is in flight, so it does not "queue immediately".
69	
70	## The mark, and the parameters in the body

72	**The mark is one label**: **`task:origin:ad-hoc`** (`mcp__github__issue_write`,

---

# /do-later — defer a change into a chained request run

The owner has spotted a change that should happen **after** the work in front of
them. Doing it now derails the session; an ordinary issue waits for somebody to
remember it. This files it as an **ad-hoc request** (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §16):
an issue the queue picks up on its own, held behind what is still in flight.

You are filing work, not doing it. Touch no source file, open no branch.

## What you write

**One issue, well defined.** The run that implements it will never see this
conversation — the issue body is the whole brief. State the change, the files or
surfaces it touches if you know them, what "done" looks like, and anything the
owner ruled out. Size it to its idea; a rename is a sentence.

**Every field a run reads is one block on the first lines of the description**,
above the marker and ahead of your prose — the waits and the parameters together,
verbatim in this spelling:

```
Blocked-by: #<what this waits on>
Not-before: <ISO instant this may first run>
Model: <opus | sonnet | haiku>
Automerge: <policy>
Task: <pack>/<task>

<!-- filed by /do-later -->

<the brief>
```

Write only the lines the deferral actually has; each is explained below. A field
further down the body still parses, but nobody editing the issue can then see what
the run will do, and a retry that rewrites `Not-before:` has no one place to write
it — #1160 carried its model six paragraphs below its waits.

The two waits compose: an issue carrying both sleeps until every blocker has
closed **and** the moment has passed.

**What issue it waits on**, first match wins:

1. the issue of the **previous `/do-later` you filed in this session** — that is
   the chain the owner asked for, each deferral behind the last;
2. otherwise the **pull request** the session's work is on, if one is open;
3. otherwise the **issue** the session is working on;
4. otherwise nothing — omit the field, and say in your reply that it queues
   immediately.

Only ever name blockers that will actually *close* — a merged PR does, a branch
does not. If you filed an earlier `/do-later` this session but no longer have its
number, find it by its marker line among the repo's open issues rather than
falling back to (2).

**What moment it waits on.** A deferral the owner words as a *time* — "check
tomorrow", "in a week", "not until after the release" — waits on an instant, and
`Blocked-by:` cannot express it. That is `Not-before:`, and it is the queue's own
wait field rather than a parameter: it is honoured whether or not the author holds
push access. Give it an ISO-8601 instant resolved against today's date
(`Not-before: 2026-08-28T09:00:00Z`) — the next scheduler run adopts the issue,
holds it blocked, and releases it on the first hourly pass after that instant.

or PR is in flight, so it does not "queue immediately".
