1	---
2	name: verify-in-production
3	description: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
4	---
5	
6	# Verify in production
7	
8	A change is finished when someone has watched it work. Most changes you can watch **now**, and
9	that is the rule — this skill is only for the rest: a change whose proof lives somewhere the
10	repo cannot see yet. You are filing the proof, not doing the work — and the proof itself runs
11	unattended: an automatic check, end to end, with a person entering
12	only where no automatic check can exist.
13	
14	## When it fires: after the merge, never before
15	
16	**The PR must have merged.** This skill runs as a step of the merge, unasked — `merge-to-main`
17	calls it once the squash has landed — and at no other moment. Not when the code is written, not
18	when the PR opens, not while review is in flight.
19	
20	The reason is that a PR can be **rejected**, and a branch that is still open can be rewritten
21	under you. Both leave a verification whose premise never reached `main`:
22	
23	- A **rewritten branch** makes the brief describe a change that no longer exists. #1121 was filed
24	  against a scope its PR then dropped; the verification was moot before the merge it waited on.
25	- A **rejected PR** is worse, because the queue cannot tell it from a merge. A blocked item
26	  releases on its blocker being *closed*, and nothing reads `merged` — so the item goes ready,
27	  reads an `In-production-when:` that can never become true, pushes `Not-before:` forward by
28	  `Retry-every:` without comment, and repeats indefinitely. No janitor rule reclaims it: the
29	  stale-ready sweep cannot see an item sleeping on a future `Not-before`, and the
30	  stuck-dependency sweep exempts an item whose blockers have closed.
31	
32	So there is no such thing as filing this early and letting the queue sort it out. Wait for the
33	merge, then read **what actually landed** — the merged diff, not the branch you remember writing.
34	
35	## First: does this file anything at all?
36	
37	Most changes **file nothing.** Run the test in this order and stop at the first answer:
38	
39	1. **Can you watch it work in this session — now, or after a wait you can sit through?**
40	   Then do that and file nothing. Not only "did you already": #1460 was filed and then
41	   hand-verified twelve minutes later, which means the artifact was readable all along and
42	   the issue was pure overhead. If it becomes readable inside the session you are in,
43	   waiting for it is cheaper than every mechanism below.
44	2. **Did a test that ran prove it?** A unit test, a CI job, an executable-requirements or UI
45	   test covering exactly the behaviour that changed. File nothing — the suite is the mechanism
46	   that comes back.
47	3. **Does the change have an observable effect at all?** A comment, a design doc, a README, a
48	   rename with no behavioural edge, a refactor a passing suite already pins. File nothing.
49	4. **Otherwise: where does its effect first become observable?** If the answer is a place and a
50	   moment — a member repo once it converges, a site once it deploys, a session once it reloads
51	   its rules — that is what you file.
52	
53	The bar is *could not be watched now*, not *would be nice to double-check*. A verification
54	filed for a change already covered by a test is a wasted run re-proving what the suite proved.
55	And the test above only files point assertions: when the merge completes a **larger element** —
56	one that earned a design doc or a phased tracking issue — the ~week-later review of how the
57	whole design fared is [production-retrospective](../production-retrospective/SKILL.md)'s
58	separate call, made beside this one.
59	
60	## Second: can the RUN read it?
61	
62	The run is an unattended session on this repository, and its reach is narrower than
63	yours: **GitHub, through its own tools, in the repositories its routine's scope names**
64	— and nothing else. There is no browser and no general egress, so a `*.github.io` page,
65	a live site's `/version.json`, a console, a dashboard and a login-walled report are all
66	unreadable to it, and so is a repository outside that scope.
67	
68	So take the read you are about to write into `Verify:` and answer, in one sentence,
69	*which tool call makes it*. If you cannot name one, the run cannot make it either — and
70	filing it anyway spends a session rediscovering that wall and then parks
71	`needs-human-action`, which is the human's-memory outcome this skill exists to avoid.
72	One executor batch spent five of its seven claimed items exactly that way (#1184, #1253,
73	#1268, #1288, #1291).
74	
75	| the read | which form |
76	|---|---|
77	| this repo's files, issues, PRs, labels, workflow runs, checks | the automatic form below |
78	| another repo's, **only** where the routine's scope names it | the automatic form below |
79	| a web page, a site, a console, a dashboard, a login wall | the human-step form |
80	
81	**The human-step form** is an ordinary issue, not a queue item: title it the same
82	`Verify in production: …`, carry `Original-issue:` and attach it as that issue's
83	sub-issue, and write the body as a checkbox per step — the exact URL to open, what to
84	look for, what counts as a pass, and what to do if it fails. **No mark, no
85	`Not-before:`, no `Retry-every:`, no `Model:`**: nothing in it is the queue's, and a
86	mark would buy only a session that parks. Assign it to whoever owns the release, and say
87	in your reply that this one needs their eyes because no runner can see the artifact.
88	
89	## What you file
90	
91	**A deferred request** — the same ad-hoc lane `/do-later` rides, so the queue does the waiting,
92	the running and the lifecycle; nothing here adds machinery beside it. One issue, titled
93	`Verify in production: <the change, in a few words>`, its body the whole brief: the run that
94	verifies will never see this conversation and may be days away. **Every field a run reads is one
95	block on the first lines of the description**, ahead of your prose — the same placement
96	[`/do-later`](../do-later/SKILL.md) files under, and what gives the retry below one place to
97	rewrite `Not-before:`. Then say what changed and why it could not be watched now.
98	
99	```
100	Original-issue: #<the change's issue>
101	In-production-when: <the concrete artifact to read, and what makes it true>
102	Verify: <what to observe, and what counts as a pass>
103	Not-before: <ISO instant just past the expected release>
104	Retry-every: <how far to push Not-before when not yet live, e.g. 1 day>
105	Model: sonnet
106	```
107	
108	No `Blocked-by:`. You are filing after the merge, so the change's PR has already closed and
109	there is nothing left to wait on but the release itself.
110	
111	- **`Original-issue:`** is where a failure lands — the issue the change was done under, which
112	  the run reopens if the verification fails. Make the verification that issue's **sub-issue**
113	  too (`mcp__github__sub_issue_write`, method `add`, `issue_number` the original,
114	  `sub_issue_id` the **id** the create call returned, not its number), so the change it proves
115	  shows what is still unproven about it — [RULES.md](../../RULES.md)' *Filing an issue that
116	  belongs under another*, applied where there is no PR left to carry the link.
117	- **`In-production-when:`** names a thing to *read*, never a duration to wait.
118	  "`missingbulb/Shepherd`'s `.claudinite-settings.json` stamps `packVersions.tidy-repo` at 8 or
119	  higher." "Any session started after this
120	  landed — check the vendored copy under `.claudinite/shared/` carries the new text." A merge
121	  is not a production condition, neither is elapsed time, and neither is anything the run
122	  cannot read.
123	- **`Verify:`** is an assertion with a pass condition, not a topic — and a read the run can
124	  actually make (the gate above): a file's content, an issue's state, a run's conclusion.
